Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review basic definitions of statistics that apply to clinical research.
Identify a hypotheses and the associated errors that can arise.
Interpret the diagnostic performance of a given test.
Compare different variables and the application of various data sets.
Determine what test to use for specific research scenarios.
Overview Definitions
Accuracy: the degree to which a measurement corresponds with its true value1
Precision: the degree to which a measurement of a variable is reproducible and produces
nearly the same value with each measurement1

Incidence: the number of newly reported cases for a given condition in a specific time period;
this number often is obtained by a prospective cohort study.1,2
Prevalence: the total number of cases of a given condition in a location at any time; this
number often is obtained by a cross-sectional study.1,2
Mean: average value of a numeric variable in a sample or population1-3
Median: value of a variable that divides a sample or population into two halves1-3
Mode: value of a data set that occurs most often in a sample or population1-3
Standard deviation: average of variability of all observations1-3
Normal distribution: also known as Gaussian distribution, in which the data vary
symmetrically2-4
In a normal distribution, the investigator is able to provide an interval within which most of the
observations are expected to distribute. Often, a confidence interval of 95% is approximately
equal to the mean plus or minus two times the standard deviation.2,3
Relative risk (risk difference): risk of an outcome in one group minus the risk in a comparison
group1-3
This factor often is used in comparing a group with known exposure with a group without
exposure. It can be calculated by comparing the incidence of a given condition in the
exposed group with the incidence in the nonexposed group.1,3 Relative risk often is used to
portray the results of a cohort study.3
Number needed to treat: absolute number of people who need to receive a treatment to
prevent the occurrence of one outcome; this number is calculated by the reciprocal of the
relative risk.1,2
Odds ratio: ratio of the odds of having a disease in a study group to the odds of having the
disease in the control group; this ratio often is used in the results of a case-control study.1-4
Sample size: subset of a specific variable for a given research study1,2
Effect size: magnitude of difference between groups to be considered meaningful; this factor
often is used in power analysis to determine the required sample size of a study.1,2
Forming a Hypothesis
Hypothesis testing confirms or refutes the statement that an observed finding occurred
through a true association between variables and not by chance alone.1,2

Type I error (alpha): The null hypothesis is rejected incorrectly. This means that the study
showed that a difference did exist between study groups when, in fact, no difference existed.2-
5
P value: The probability, by chance, of obtaining a given effect as large as or larger if the null
hypothesis is true.2-5
Type II error (beta): The null hypothesis is accepted incorrectly. This means that the study
showed that no difference existed in the study groups when, in fact, a difference did exist.2,4
Power (1-beta): The probability of finding a significant association when one truly exists1,2,4

Forming a Hypothesis
After variables are established, the investigator tests whether a true difference exists
between the variable of the intervention group and that of the control group.
Traditionally, this factor is portrayed by the null hypothesis, which states that no
difference exists between the two groups. The goal is to decide to accept or reject the
null hypothesis.2,3,5
Alpha is useful in comparing to the P value, which denotes the observing differences
between the two groups. If the P value is less than alpha, then the decision is made to
reject the null hypothesis. If the P value is greater than alpha, then the result observed is
small compared with what could have occurred by chance alone. Most commonly, the P
value is set at 0.05; however, this distinction is purely arbitrary. A P value may be
statistically significant but not clinically important or relevant.1,2,4
Beta is useful in regard to the power of the study, which denotes the potential of a study
to find significant association among study groups, if one truly exists.4,5 Because alpha
should be small, the power should be large, for example 0.9 or 0.95. By typical
convention, a power greater than or equal to 0.8 is sufficient to identify a significant
association.4
Diagnostic Performance

Sensitivity: The probability that identifies a patient has a given condition in those who truly
have the condition1,2,4
Specificity: The probability that a test result will be negative in a patient without a given
condition1,2,4
Positive predictive value: The proportion of subjects with positive tests who have the disease1-
3
Negative predictive value: The proportion of patients with negative tests who do not have the
disease1-3
Table 1 shows a 2 × 2 table depicting the calculations for sensitivity, specificity, positive
predictive value, and negative predictive value. True positive (a) represents the patients who
truly have a given condition and accurately test positive. False positive (b) represents patients
who test positive but do not have a given condition. True negative (c) indicates patients who
accurately test negative for a condition. False negative (d) indicates patients who have a given
condition but inaccurately test negative.

Receiver operating characteristic curve: A graph that depicts the trade-off between sensitivity
and specificity at each point (Figure 1).
Likelihood ratio: An analytic tool designed to indicate the possibility that a certain test result
would be expected for a person with a certain condition compared with a given test result for
a patient without that condition1,2
Figure 1 Graph shows the receiver operating characteristic curve, with sensitivity on the Y axis
and 1-specificity (false-positive rate) on the X axis. This curve can be used if a diagnostic test
yields continuous results. The investigator can decipher several cutoff points and plot the data.
An ideal test, shown at the upper left corner of the graph, would represent 100% true-positive
results and no false-positive results. A worthless test follows the diagonal line and shows that
the true-positive results are equal to the false-positive results. The area under the curve
ranges from 0.5, which represents a worthless test, to 1.0, which represents a perfect test.

Diagnostic Performance
Sensitivity is useful during screening to rule out patients. A highly sensitive test rules out
patients who do not have the condition with confidence.1,2,4 A common pneumonic
device used to remember sensitivity is SnOUT (sensitive test when Negative rules OUT).2
A highly specific test will confirm a given condition with a high degree of confidence.1-3 A
common pneumonic device used to remember the specificity for a test, to confirm a
given condition is SpIN (Specific tests rule IN).2
The likelihood ratio of a positive test can be calculated as sensitivity/(1-specificity), which
is the probability of a true positive divided by the probability of a false positive. The
likelihood ratio of a negative test can be calculated by (1-sensitivity)/specificity.1,2 A
likelihood ratio closer to 1 represents a test that provides little information. A likelihood
ratio that is close to 0 represents a test result that is useful for ruling out a disease. If the
likelihood ratio is a higher value, then the test is better for confirming a disease.1
Types of Variables
Types of categorical variables
Dichotomous: A variable with two possible values, such as yes or no, male or female, positive
or negative, present or absent1,2,5
Nominal: A variable that is not categorized in order. Examples include labeling various
surgical implants A, B, and C.1,2,5
Ordinal data: A type of categorical variable in which the values have a logical order but
cannot be quantified. Examples include cancer stages or injury grades.1,2,5
Types of numeric variables

Discrete: A variable that takes an integer variable1,2,5
These variables have a set scale of fixed units (eg, heart rate). Discrete data may resemble
continuous data in certain instances.1
Continuous: A variable that is quantified on an infinite scale1,2,5
Continuous data can be transformed into other types of variables (discrete, ordinal, or
nominal) by grouping observations.1,2 Examples include postoperative range of motion and
degrees of anteversion.
Statistical Inference
Definition: Analysis of data performed to draw conclusions from research study data4
Parametric data: Continuous data that are normally distributed2,4
If data are parametric, the standard deviation is essentially the average from the mean of all
observations. This also is known as Gaussian distribution.2-4
Confidence interval: A range of values used in descriptive studies that measures the precision
of a sample estimate1-3
In contrast to the P value, which denotes statistical significance, the confidence interval is
preset by the investigator and may portray information, including the significance of the
findings and the magnitude of differences.1,3 The confidence interval often is arbitrarily set
at 95%.1-3 The width of the confidence interval depends on the sample size of the study1,3
(Figure 2; Resource 1).
Nonparametric data: Continuous data that are not normally distributed. This often is referred
to as skewed data2,3 (Figure 3).
Correlation coefficient: A measure of the strength of the linear association between two
variables1-3
This analytic tool can be used if predictor variables (risk factors) and outcome variables are
continuous.1,3 It varies between -1 and +1. The closer the value is to 1, the stronger the
association is between the two variables. Negative values indicate inverse correlation; as one
variable increases, the other variable decreases. As the value approaches 0, the association
between the two variables becomes weaker.3

Study Types
Student t tests (Table 2)
Used for continuous data with a normal distribution of two independent groups4,5
Paired t tests
Used for continuous data with a normal distribution for paired samples of two independent
variables4
An example is preoperative and postoperative range of motion of the knee, in which one
group receives a posterior-stabilized knee prosthesis and the other receives a cruciate-
retaining knee prosthesis.
Analysis of variance
Continuous data with normal distribution used to compare the means among three or more
independent groups2,4
Mann-Whitney U test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
Used for nonparametric tests comparing two independent groups2,3
Kruskal-Wallis test
Used for nonparametric data for three or more independent groups2,3
Sign test
Used for nonparametric data for one or two independent groups2,3
Pearson product-moment correlation
Used to determine associations for parametric variables2
Spearman rank-order correlation2,3
Used to determine associations for nonparametric variables
 Chi-squared test
Used for two or more categorical variables1-3
Can be used for parametric or nonparametric variables
Fisher exact test2
Used for categorical variables if the sample sizes are small (five or less) or the frequency in a
group is low
Kendall rank-correlation
Used to determine associations between ordinal variables2
